title: Group, measure and reshape
summary: Turn a raw request log into answers: Group-Object, Measure-Object, calculated properties, -PipelineVariable and Export-Csv.

steps.title: Counting and summing without a loop
body: `~/data/requests.csv` is a load balancer export: one row per request with `Time, Method, Path, Status, Ms`.
`Import-Csv` turns each row into an object whose properties are the column names.
```powershell
$log = Import-Csv ~/data/requests.csv
$log | Group-Object Status | Sort-Object Count -Descending     # how many of each status code
$log | Measure-Object -Property Ms -Average -Maximum           # average and slowest response
- **`Group-Object Prop`** emits one `GroupInfo` per distinct value: `Name` (the value), `Count`, and `Group` (the
objects in it). `-NoElement` leaves `Group` out when you only want the counts.
- **`Measure-Object -Property Prop`** with `-Sum`, `-Average`, `-Minimum`, `-Maximum` (or `-AllStats`) returns one
object with those numbers. Without `-Property` it just counts.
**Watch out:** every value from `Import-Csv` is a **string**. Measure-Object converts to numbers for you, but
`Sort-Object Ms` sorts *text* (`'99'` after `'1200'`). Sort by `{ [int]$_.Ms }` when the column is numeric.

stages.note: 400 row objects (the first four are shown). Every property is a **string**, even `Status` and `Ms`.
One object per distinct status, in order of the value. `Name` is the status value, `Count` how many rows had it.
`Count` is a real integer, so this sort is numeric.
A calculated property renames `Name` to `Status`, so the CSV you export says what it means.

steps.explain: Strings group by their own value. `web` appears three times, so its group sorts first, and `-ExpandProperty Name` prints the plain value.

steps.title: Calculated properties: reshape on the way through
body: `Select-Object` (and `Sort-Object`, `Format-Table`, `Group-Object`) accept a **hashtable** instead of a property name:
```powershell
Get-ChildItem ~/data -Recurse -File |
Select-Object Name,
@{ Name = 'MB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.Length / 1MB, 1) } },
@{ Name = 'AgeDays'; Expression = { ((Get-Date) - $_.LastWriteTime).Days } }
`Name` (or `n`, `Label`, `l`) is the new property's name; `Expression` (or `e`) is a script block where `$_` is the
object coming in. Sorting by an expression works the same way: `Sort-Object { [int]$_.Ms } -Descending`.
**`-PipelineVariable` (`-pv`)** saves the object of an earlier stage under a name, so a later stage can still see it
after the pipe has moved on to other objects:
```powershell
Get-ChildItem ~/logs -Directory -PipelineVariable dir |
Get-ChildItem -File |
Select-Object @{ n = 'Folder'; e = { $dir.Name } }, Name, Length
In the last stage `$_` is a *file*; `$dir` is still the folder it came from.

steps.prompt: Add a calculated column `KB` (the size in KB, no decimals) next to the name.
steps.explain: The keys are `Name` and `Expression` (short forms `n` and `e`). Inside the expression `$_` is the object coming down the pipe.

steps.title: Status codes for the incident review
prompt: For this morning's incident review, count the requests in `~/data/requests.csv` **per status code**, and export the
result to `~/answers/status.csv` with exactly two columns, **`Status`** and **`Count`**, biggest count first.
`Export-Csv -Path FILE` writes objects as CSV; the property names become the header row.

checks.name: status.csv has Status and Count, right counts, biggest first
checks.fail: Not quite. The check's message above says what it found.

hints: `Import-Csv ~/data/requests.csv | Group-Object Status -NoElement | Sort-Object Count -Descending` gives the counts. Its columns are `Count` and `Name`.
Rename `Name` with a calculated property: `Select-Object @{ Name = 'Status'; Expression = { $_.Name } }, Count`.
End with `| Export-Csv -Path ~/answers/status.csv`, then `Get-Content ~/answers/status.csv` to look at it.
solution: $log | Group-Object Status -NoElement | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object @{ Name = 'Status'; Expression = { $_.Name } }, Count | Export-Csv -Path ~/answers/status.csv
steps.explain: In PowerShell 7, `Export-Csv` writes UTF-8 and no `#TYPE` line. Windows PowerShell 5.1 adds a `#TYPE System.Management.Automation.PSCustomObject` first line unless you pass `-NoTypeInformation`, which is why you see that flag in so many older scripts (in 7 it does nothing).

steps.prompt: Which pipeline gives the **slowest** request (highest `Ms`) from `$log = Import-Csv ~/data/requests.csv`?
steps.explain: `Ms` is a string, so `Sort-Object Ms` sorts text: `'99'` comes before `'1200'`. Casting in a sort expression makes it numeric. `Measure-Object -Maximum` gives the right *number* but not the request it belongs to.

steps.prompt: Match each question to the cmdlet that answers it.
pairs: What is the average response time?
Which properties does this object have?
Rename a column for the report

steps.title: Which endpoints are slow?
prompt: The team wants a table of endpoints by speed. Export `~/answers/slow.csv` with one row **per `Path`** and exactly these
- `Requests`: how many requests that path had;
- `AvgMs`: their average `Ms`, **rounded to a whole number**.

checks.name: slow.csv has Path, Requests, AvgMs, slowest first
checks.fail: Not quite. The check's message above says what it found.

hints: Group by path: `Import-Csv ~/data/requests.csv | Group-Object Path`. Each group's `Group` holds that path's rows.
For one group `$g`: `($g.Group | Measure-Object Ms -Average).Average` is the average. `[math]::Round(...)` makes it whole.

`Select-Object @{ n = 'Path'; e = { $_.Name } }, @{ n = 'Requests'; e = { $_.Count } }, @{ n = 'AvgMs'; e = { [math]::Round(($_.Group | Measure-Object Ms -Average).Average) } } | Sort-Object AvgMs -Descending | Export-Csv ~/answers/slow.csv`
solution: $byPath | Select-Object @{ n = 'Path'; e = { $_.Name } }, @{ n = 'Requests'; e = { $_.Count } }, @{ n = 'AvgMs'; e = { [math]::Round(($_.Group | Measure-Object Ms -Average).Average) } } | Sort-Object AvgMs -Descending | Export-Csv -Path ~/answers/slow.csv
explain: `/api/search` is the slow one, at about 790 ms on average. In a real review you would also want the 95th
percentile: averages hide the slow tail. Sort the group's `Ms` as numbers and take the value 95% of the way down.
